slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: Used to screen for or diagnose type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, and to monitor glucose control in people who already have diabetes or prediabetes. It is not used to diagnose type 1 diabetes, although it may be used for monitoring.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: Blood glucose attaches to hemoglobin in red blood cells: the higher the glucose, the more hemoglobin becomes glucose-coated. The glucose stays attached for the life of the red cell (about three months), so A1C reflects average glucose over the past 2–3 months.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: A1C is a weighted average: glucose levels in the preceding 30 days contribute more to the result than those 90–120 days earlier. Clinically significant changes in glucose therefore show up in A1C without waiting 120 days for red-cell turnover.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits
rows: People who are not pregnant — IFCC: 39–47 mmol/mol (ADA, Table 2.2). Pregnancy uses different cutoffs for some tests.
People who are not pregnant — 6.5% or above (IFCC: ≥ 48 mmol/mol; ADA, Table 2.1). Diagnosis is usually confirmed with a second test. Pregnancy uses different cutoffs for some tests.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: High: A high A1C is a sign of high blood glucose from diabetes. Because more than one test is often used for diagnosis, a raised result is usually followed by a repeat A1C or a different test, most often a fasting blood glucose test or an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No fasting is needed: the person can eat and drink before the test, and blood can be drawn at any time of day.
Interferences: Certain medicines, such as opioids and some HIV medicines, may affect the result, so all medicines taken should be reported. Pregnancy may also affect the result.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Conditions that change red-cell life span—recent blood loss, sickle cell disease, erythropoietin treatment, hemodialysis or transfusion—can change A1C. Very low iron (iron-deficiency anemia) can give a falsely high A1C, and kidney failure or liver disease can also cause false results.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Common hemoglobinopathies (e.g., HbS, HbC, HbE, HbSC, elevated HbF) can falsely raise or lower A1C, depending on the variant and the assay method. NIDDK advises against using A1C in patients with HbSS, HbCC or HbSC.

Suspect a hemoglobinopathy when A1C is unexpected or at odds with other diabetes tests, is below 4% or above 15%, differs from self-monitored glucose, or changes markedly after the laboratory changes its A1C method.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Limitations: A1C should not be used to diagnose type 1 diabetes, gestational diabetes or cystic fibrosis–related diabetes.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: For diagnosis, a venous sample goes to a laboratory using an NGSP-certified method. Point-of-care A1C may be used for diagnosis only with devices approved for diagnosis (FDA) in certified (CLIA) laboratories performing moderate- or higher-complexity testing, by trained staff (ADA 2.2b); other point-of-care results are not used for diagnosis.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: A1C and blood glucose tests do not always agree: a glucose test may show diabetes when A1C does not, and vice versa. For this reason, tests are repeated before a diagnosis is made.

A1C does not show sudden, temporary rises or falls in glucose. Re-measuring the same sample can give a slightly different result; NIDDK’s example is that 6.8% on one test could read 6.4–7.2% on a repeat.

slides.title: Fructosamine
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood

What it is used for: According to NIDDK, fructosamine (or glycated albumin) may be considered as another measure of average glucose in patients with hemoglobinopathies when an accurate A1C cannot be obtained—for example in HbSS, HbCC or HbSC, where A1C should not be used.
Physiology: The fructosamine test measures glucose molecules linked to protein molecules in the blood. The assay is also called glycated serum protein.

slides.title: Fructosamine
bullets: Limitations: Fructosamine reflects a much shorter period than A1C—usually about 2–3 weeks, versus the preceding 3 months for A1C—so the two tests describe different time windows.

NIDDK patient information gives fructosamine as an example of alternative tests that scientists are working on for people with hemoglobin variants; it shows average glucose over about 3 weeks. Whether it is an option is for the doctor to decide.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 (126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 h); 75 g OGTT 2-hour ≥11.1 (200); HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP/DCCT); random ≥11.1 with symptoms; without unequivocal hyperglycemia – two abnormal results mmol/L (venous plasma)

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: in most non-pregnant adults <7% (53 mmol/mol), individualized %

slides.title: A patient with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) needs an assessment of average glucose. What does NIDDK advise?
options: Use A1C as usual — hemoglobin variants do not affect it, so no alternative test such as fructosamine is needed.
Do not use A1C; consider alternatives such as glycated serum protein (fructosamine) or glycated albumin.
Repeat A1C after an overnight fast to remove the interference, then interpret it as usual.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: NIDDK advises against A1C in HbSS, HbCC and HbSC and suggests considering alternative tests.

Basis: NIDDK professional page: do not use A1C in HbSS, HbCC or HbSC; consider glycated serum protein or glycated albumin.

slides.title: A nonpregnant person without symptoms has an A1C in the diabetes range. What should happen before a diagnosis is made?
options: Nothing more — a single A1C in the diabetes range is enough.
Confirm the result right away with a point-of-care A1C device at the bedside.
Repeat testing on a different day with A1C or another diabetes test.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: without symptoms, the diagnosis is confirmed by a repeat test on a different day.

Basis: NIDDK: without symptoms, an A1C showing diabetes or prediabetes should be confirmed by a repeat test on a different day; ADA: point-of-care A1C may be used for diagnosis only on a device approved for diagnosis in a certified laboratory (2.2b).

slides.title: Over roughly what period does fructosamine reflect average blood glucose?
options: About 2–3 weeks
About 3 months
Only glucose at the moment of sampling
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: NIDDK states fructosamine usually reflects about 2–3 weeks of average glucose.

Basis: NIDDK: fructosamine and glycated albumin reflect a much shorter period than A1C, usually about 2–3 weeks.

slides.title: In which situation do NIDDK professional materials suggest considering fructosamine?
options: In pregnant patients, as the standard test used to diagnose gestational diabetes.
In all patients, as a routine replacement for A1C in diabetes management.
In patients with hemoglobinopathies when an accurate A1C cannot be obtained.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: this is the situation in which NIDDK suggests considering fructosamine or glycated albumin.

Basis: NIDDK: when an accurate A1C cannot be obtained in a hemoglobinopathy, fructosamine or glycated albumin may be considered; gestational diabetes is checked with the glucose challenge test or OGTT.

slides.title: Fructosamines are:
options: Bind fructose to proteins
Mucopolysaccharide
Glycated albumin
Glycolipid

slides.title: Determining glycosylated hemoglobin?
bullets: 1. HbA1c is the non-enzymatic attachment of glucose to valine at the N-terminus of the hemoglobin β chain (glycation); it reflects average glycemia over the lifespan of the erythrocyte (~120 days), more so in the recent months.
2. Methods: ion-exchange HPLC, boronate affinity chromatography, immunoassay (immunoturbidimetry), enzymatic method; for diagnosis only a method that is NGSP-certified and standardized to DCCT.
3. Units: NGSP % and IFCC mmol/mol (the IFCC reference method – N-terminal hexapeptides of the β chain); 6.5% ≈ 48 mmol/mol.
4. Sample: whole venous blood with EDTA; fasting is not required.

slides.title: Determining glycosylated hemoglobin?
bullets: 5. Interferences: Hb variants (HbS, HbC, HbE, HbD) and high HbF – method-dependent; conditions altering erythrocyte lifespan (hemolysis, blood loss/transfusion, iron deficiency and its treatment, CKD, pregnancy) falsely change the result – in that case glucose or fructosamine.
6. Interpretation: <5.7% normal, 5.7–6.4% prediabetes, ≥6.5% diabetes (with confirmation); treatment target in most adults <7%.

slides.title: Determining glucose and glycated hemoglobin?
bullets: 1. Glucose: in venous plasma by enzymatic methods (hexokinase – the most specific; glucose oxidase–peroxidase); preventing glycolysis – rapid centrifugation or a tube with an inhibitor.
2. Diagnostic thresholds of glucose: fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L – diabetes, 5.6–6.9 – impaired fasting glucose (ADA); 75 g OGTT at 2 hours ≥11.1 – diabetes, 7.8–11.0 – impaired tolerance.
3. HbA1c: HPLC, boronate affinity, immunoassay or enzymatic method; NGSP-certified, DCCT-standardized; ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol) – diabetes, 5.7–6.4% – prediabetes.

slides.title: Determining glucose and glycated hemoglobin?
bullets: 4. Advantage of HbA1c – no fasting required, little day-to-day variability; disadvantage – unreliable in hemoglobinopathies, anemia, changed erythrocyte lifespan.
5. If the results of two tests disagree, the test exceeding the threshold is confirmed by repeating it.

slides.title: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Methods of determining glycosylated hemoglobin, glucose?
bullets: 1. Diagnostic criteria: fasting venous plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 75 g OGTT at 2 hours ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%, random ≥11.1 with symptoms; the confirmation rule.
2. Glucose methods: hexokinase (close to reference level, 340 nm), glucose oxidase–peroxidase; preanalytics – glycolysis, rapid centrifugation; glucometers only for monitoring.
3. HbA1c methods: ion-exchange HPLC, boronate affinity, immunoassay, enzymatic; NGSP/IFCC standardization; interference from Hb variants and erythrocyte lifespan.

slides.title: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Methods of determining glycosylated hemoglobin, glucose?
bullets: 4. Additional markers: autoantibodies and C-peptide (type 1/2), fructosamine, ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate), albuminuria (ACR).
5. Quality: two-level control, Westgard rules, external quality control; report the result in the correct units – mmol/L and mg/dL.
